facts.statement: Andrewsornis is currently known as the largest member of the subfamily Patagornithinae, reaching a height of 1.8 meters and weighing between 60 and 89 kilograms.
facts.quote: Andrewsornis is so far the largest member of the subfamily Patagornithinae, having a height of 1.8 m and weighing up to 60 - 89 kg.

facts.statement: The lower jaw of Andrewsornis measures 39 centimeters in length and is slimmer than that of Phorusrhacos.
facts.quote: the lower jaw is 39 cm long and slimmer than Phorusrhacos.

facts.statement: Fossils of Andrewsornis were first discovered on September 18, 1923, by fossil collector John Bernard Abbott in Cabeza Blanca, Chubut Province, southern Argentina.
facts.quote: Fossils of Andrewsornis were first discovered on 18 September 1923 by fossil collector John Bernard Abbott in Cabeza Blanca in the province of Chubut, Patagonia in southern Argentina.

facts.statement: Paleontologist Bryan Patterson scientifically described the remains as a new genus and species named Andrewsornis abbotti in 1941.
facts.quote: In 1941, paleontologist Bryan Patterson scientifically described the remains as belonging to a new genus and species of phorusrhacid, which he named Andrewsornis abbotti.

facts.statement: Fossils of Andrewsornis have been found in the Sarmiento Formation and possibly the Agua de la Piedra Formation.
facts.quote: Fossils have been found in the Sarmiento Formation, and possibly the Agua de la Piedra Formation.

facts.statement: Andrewsornis lived between 29 and 21 million years ago, spanning the Rupelian to Aquitanian stages.
facts.quote: Time range: Rupelian to Aquitanian (29 to 21 million years ago)

facts.statement: In 2003, Herculano Alvarenga and Elizabeth Höfling created the subfamily Patagornithinae to include Andrewsornis and Andalgalornis.
facts.quote: In 2003 during their redescription of phorusrhacidae, Herculano Alvarenga and Elizabeth Hofling created a new subfamily, Patagornithinae, with Patagornis as the type genus, that included Andrewsornis and Andalgalornis.

facts.statement: A 2015 phylogenetic analysis by Degrange et al. placed Andrewsornis in a merged Phorusrhacinae clade in polytomy with Physornis and Phorusrhacos.
facts.quote: However, a phylogenetic analysis in 2015 by Degrange et al. found Andrewsornis in a merged Phorusrhacinae and in polytomy with Physornis and Phorusrhacos as well.

rejected.statement: Andrewsornis was an extinct genus of giant, flightless, predatory birds belonging to the family Phorusrhacidae, also known as terror birds.
rejected.quote: Andrewsornis is an extinct genus of giant flightless predatory birds of the family Phorusrhacidae or "terror birds" that lived in Oligocene Argentina.

rejected.quote: The strata of the Cabeza Blanca where the fossils were found corresponds to the Deseado Formation, which comes from the Deseado SALMA (South American land mammal age) and the middle-upper Oligocene.

rejected.quote: Based on osteohistological analysis of its hindlimbs, Andrewsornis exhibited an uninterrupted growth life history strategy, similar to that of other large and flightless neognaths but differing from that of megafaunal palaeognath birds.

rejected.quote: Additionally, the study stated that Aucornis solidus, a species described in 1898 by paleontologist Florentino Ameghino on the basis of a single phalanx, is likely a synonym, of Andrewsornis. However, this cannot be proven due to the lack of diagnostic traits for phalanges.
